Approach (chosen to be provably flat-foldable): a "stacked-cell" base.

Take a square lattice of flap tips rotated 45 degrees: tips at (0.2i, 0.2j) with i+j even, i,j in 0..5, giving 18 tips (17 are needed). Each tip owns a diamond cell of side s = 0.2*sqrt(2) = 0.282843, bounded by the 45-degree lines x+y = 0.2, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 1.8 and x-y = -0.6, -0.2, 0.2, 0.6.

Fold sequence (every step is a simple fold of the whole stack, so a valid layer order exists):
1. Accordion-pleat along the x+y lines.
2. Accordion-pleat along the x-y lines. This stacks every cell (whole or partial) onto one diamond.
3. Fold the stack along one diagonal of the diamond.
4. Fold it along the remaining half-diagonal.

Every cell becomes the same right triangle. Its apex is the cell centre, which is the flap tip, and its hypotenuse is the cell boundary, which lies on the axis. The cell diagonals join up into the full horizontal and vertical lines x, y = 0.2k.

I worked out the M/V assignment from that fold sequence and checked it at every interior vertex:
- Each degree-8 vertex has 5 creases of one type and 3 of the other.
- Each degree-4 cell centre has 3 of one type and 1 of the other.
- All angles are 45 degrees, so Kawasaki holds.

Resulting tree: a star of 18 flaps, each of length s/2 = 0.141421. Every pair of tips is s = 0.282843 apart. Any 17 tips can be matched to the leaves. The largest target distance is 12.5 (antenna to tail fan), so the scale is m = 0.282843 / 12.5 = 0.0226 (approximately).

I chose a conservative design that is guaranteed to be valid: a 3x3 kaleidoscopic grid base. The target tree has 14 leaves, so I used a base with 16 flaps.

How it folds. It is a sequence of four simple folds, so it is flat-foldable by construction:
1. Accordion-pleat along x=1/3 (V) and x=2/3 (M).
2. Accordion-pleat the strip along y=1/3 and y=2/3. These are V/M on face-up columns and M/V on the face-down middle column.
3. Fold the 9-layer square of side 1/3 along one diagonal.
4. Fold the resulting triangle along its altitude.

Each cell therefore gets both diagonals. The M/V assignments come from the orientation of each layer at the time of each fold. I checked by hand that Maekawa holds at the cell centres (3:1) and at a sample of four interior grid vertices (5:3). Kawasaki holds everywhere because all angles are 45 degrees.

What it makes. All 36 quarter-cell triangles stack onto one right isosceles triangle with base 1/3 and height 1/6. The 16 grid points become flap tips at the two base corners. The cell centres and edge midpoints form one connected hub. The stick figure is a star with 16 legs, each of length L = 1/6.

Scale. Every pair of tips is 2L = 1/3 apart. The largest target distance is between prim_l2 and a hind leg: 2.5+3+3+4 = 12.5. So m = (1/3)/12.5 ≈ 0.0267. Any assignment of the 14 target leaves to 14 of the 16 tips gives the same result. This is far below an optimal packing, but the pattern should fold validly.

Approach (safe, guaranteed flat-foldable): a 45-degree "map fold" on the diagonal grid through the 4x4 lattice of points (i/3, j/3).

- Family A: lines x+y = n/3 (n=1..5), folded as an accordion (n odd V, n even M), each line uniform.
- Family B: lines x-y = c/3 (c=-2..2). Reflection across any family-A line preserves x-y, so after the first accordion every family-B line lies in the same place in all layers. Folding them as a second accordion makes each family-B segment flip assignment between strips: the segment in strip k = floor(3(x+y)) is V if (c+k) is even, M otherwise.
Every interior vertex is a 90-degree degree-4 vertex with a 3-1 split, so Maekawa and Kawasaki hold. Folding one family first and then the other gives a valid layer order.

Folded state: a diamond whose axis runs from the image of the even lattice points (i+j even) to the image of the odd ones. Axis length is 1/3. The square centres and edge midpoints of the 1/3-cells map to the middle. The level set at the middle is the connected grid x, y = (2k+1)/6, so it is one hub. Each of the 16 lattice points is a separate flap tip at distance 1/6 from the hub. The tree is a 16-leaf star with legs of length 1/6, and every pair of tips is 1/3 apart.

Match any 13 tips to the 13 target leaves. The largest target leaf distance is 9 (for example mandible to abdomen_tip, or mandible to leg3), so the scale is m = (1/3)/9 = 0.037037.

Design idea (box pleated on a 10-grid): split the square at x = 0.4 into two rectangles, 0.4 x 1 and 0.6 x 1, and give each one its own "nearest-edge" (fish-type) collapse. In each rectangle there is a full vertical centre crease (x = 0.2 or x = 0.7) plus 45-degree creases from each corner to the skeleton points: (0.2,0.2) and (0.2,0.8) on the left, (0.7,0.3) and (0.7,0.7) on the right. The line x = 0.4 is not creased. The two folded stacks sit side by side, at g in [0,0.2] and g in [-0.3,0]. In each stack, the half on one side of the centre crease folds onto the other half, and then both corner triangles fold up over the stack along the diagonals. This is a series of simple folds, so a valid layer order exists. Each interior vertex has degree 4 with angles 45/45/135/135 and three creases of one type to one of the other, so Maekawa and Kawasaki both hold.

Folded height h (the axis is the paper's y direction after folding): all six vertices on the paper's edge are flap tips. (0,0), (0.4,0) and (1,0) sit at h = 0; (0,1), (0.4,1) and (1,1) sit at h = 1.
Tree: tips (0,0) and (0.4,0) meet at h = 0.2. Tip (1,0) joins at h = 0.3. A body runs from 0.3 to 0.7, and the top is the mirror image.
Tip distances:
- (0,0)-(0.4,0) = 0.4
- (0,0)-(1,0) and (0.4,0)-(1,0) = 0.6
- the top cluster has the same distances
- every bottom-to-top distance = 1.0

Matching:
- hind_left = (0,0), hind_right = (0.4,0), tail_tip = (1,0)
- front_left = (0,1), front_right = (0.4,1), head = (1,1)

Required at m = 0.1:
- hind-left to hind-right: 4m = 0.4, have 0.4
- hind foot to tail: 6m = 0.6, have 0.6
- front pairs: 4m = 0.4, have 0.4 or more
- front to hind: 7m = 0.7, have 1
- head or front foot to tail: 9m = 0.9, have 1

Scale m = 0.1.
(Note: the design is plain box pleating. I did not include a Pythagorean stretch, because I kept the pattern to one whose flat-foldability I could check by hand.)
